name: Chloe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing, and your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and run a loader at a large mine. I walk round it before the shift, check the bucket pins, and load trucks to the weight we’ve been given. I like doing a clean job with the crew I know, but the early starts make the rest of the day disappear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the mine like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Peter works at a hardware shop, and our children are grown and have their own homes. We put aside about four months of bills, and I want to keep earning until retirement is actually affordable. I have a vocational certificate, not a lifetime guarantee from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a small improvement to paperwork is fine if it stays out of the operator’s sightline. I don’t use AI tools myself; our paper checks have caught loose pins for years. Let the office save its minutes and leave us room to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be glad the loader and my roster remain much the same. Peter’s shop hours have been steady, though four months of savings would not fund a long illness or an early exit. I would not mistake unchanged technology for a secure retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the paper walkaround sheet and load the same assigned trucks. I’d put thirty from each pay packet into our savings account if the household bills allow it. In the first year after the minor software change, I’d report any wrong load figure to the weighbridge clerk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about the mine day and somewhat tired of new office systems. I know how to do this job. Retirement money would stay on my mind, as it does now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a paper check catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I saw a fresh line of grease near a bucket pin and asked the fitter to look. The loader stayed parked until he cleared it, which was better than losing the bucket halfway through a load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only thirty each pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter and I still pay for the car and help at our church kitchen on Saturdays. Thirty is an amount I can promise without pretending our costs are lower than they are.

say: I’d accept **shorter paperwork** while keeping the loader checks familiar.
I would still use the **paper walkaround** to spot equipment faults.
think: I expect my **roster** to continue, but four months of savings cannot fund early retirement.
Peter’s **shop hours** are steady for now.
do: Keep the **paper inspection** and load assigned trucks.
Put **thirty** from each pay packet into savings if bills allow.
Report wrong **load figures** to the weighbridge clerk.
feel: **Calm** about the work, while retirement costs remain in view.
S0.quote: I would not mistake unchanged technology for a secure retirement.
fieldNote: Chloe trusts the **paper walkaround** because it has exposed real faults, and she does not use AI tools.
Her savings decision is **modest** because ordinary household costs and commitments continue even in a mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep inspecting the loader on paper and loading assigned trucks
Save thirty from each pay packet if household bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that software doing the buying and scheduling will not lift a bucket today. The clerks deserve straight answers about their posts, and operators deserve schedules checked by someone who knows the pit. I would ask our foreman to keep the old load sheet until the new numbers are proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry that management will call the change efficient and then demand more loads per shift. I’m not eager to learn a new screen to prove something I already do properly. Robots come slowly here, but a mine can change its staffing plan before a robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman for a printed comparison of old and new load targets at the next crew meeting. I’d keep my loader shifts and log any unsafe target beside the weighbridge ticket. In the first year, I’d postpone replacing our dining table and put the money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy because my pay looks safe for now but the pressure on the shift could rise. I’d be angry for the clerks if their posts shrink. Peter would hear about it over supper, not from a public complaint online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an unsafe target look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the new plan ignores time lost to a blocked haul road, a loader can rush a truck and send it overweight. I’d keep the weighbridge ticket and ask the foreman to correct that target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay a table if your wages continue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old table still holds our supper plates. A few hundred in the bank gives Peter and me more room if the mine starts trimming shifts later.

say: I’d say **scheduling software** cannot lift a bucket or know every pit delay.
I’d ask the foreman to check **new targets** before using them.
think: My wages may continue while management pushes **more loads** into each shift.
I worry about the **clerks** whose work changes first.
do: Request a printed **target comparison** at the crew meeting.
Keep loading and log **unsafe targets** beside weighbridge tickets.
Delay the **dining table** purchase and bank the money.
feel: **Uneasy** about rising shift pressure and colleagues losing work.
S1.quote: The old table still holds our supper plates.
fieldNote: Chloe views **office automation** through the targets it might impose on her loader shift, rather than through the software itself.
She delays a **table purchase** as a small buffer, while still expecting wages over the next few years.

steps.text: Keep loader shifts and record unsafe targets beside weighbridge tickets
Bank the money reserved for a new dining table

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2028 could wipe out office tasks, and robots able to load trucks follow around 2031. I would ask the mine for a written date before anybody tells me to be grateful for three more years. If they want people to leave, they should state the terms plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 60 when the office changes and 63 when a robot could take the loader. I expected to work longer than that; four months of bills is not a bridge to retirement. Peter’s hardware-shop wage could help, but it would not replace my mine pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask payroll this month for my actual retirement balance and any redundancy terms. I’d look at loader jobs at the two nearby sites and apply if one is advertised with a longer contract, though robots may reach those mines too. In 2029 I’d keep working my assigned loader shifts and cut our paid holidays to protect cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious and angry at being asked to plan from guesses. I have work for the moment and a couple of places to ask, so I’m not without a plan. I would pray with Peter at home, but I would still open the bills afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a nearby mine really protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a robot could reach the other site as well. An actual contract might buy us time, and I would read its length before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our grown children we can manage this month but will stop paying for family holidays. They have their own households, and I do not want to make my wages their emergency.

say: I’d ask for a written **robot date** and clear leaving terms.
I would tell coworkers that **2031 loaders** threaten our paid shifts.
think: At **63**, I could lose the loader wages I expected to earn before retirement became affordable.
Peter’s **shop wage** would not replace mine.
do: Request my **retirement balance** and redundancy terms this month.
Apply for an advertised **nearby loader job** with a longer contract.
Keep loader shifts in **2029** and stop paid holidays.
feel: **Anxious** about losing mine pay, while still able to work and look for openings.
S2.quote: I expected to work longer than that; four months of bills is not a bridge to retirement.
fieldNote: Chloe sees **2031 robots** as a direct threat to loader wages she expected to earn beyond age 63.
She would seek **nearby work** only with a real longer contract, knowing another mine is no permanent refuge.

steps.text: Keep assigned loader shifts through 2029 if available
Apply for a nearby advertised loader job with a longer contract
Stop paying for family holidays after the 2028 change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a five-year warning is worth something if we can see the machine orders. Thinking AI reaches the office in 2031 and loading robots around 2034, when I’d be 66. I would want the mine to offer real apprenticeships for younger workers, rather than a speech about adapting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be ready to stop at 66, but I cannot say that before seeing our retirement numbers. Peter may cut his hardware-shop hours by then, and our grown children have their own bills. I do not want to take a course that costs more than it returns at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get a retirement estimate from payroll and sit with Peter over our bank statements this winter. I’d ask the foreman each year what loader work remains and continue my shifts while it is available. In 2032 I’d compare our monthly costs with any offered exit payment before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, but there is time for sensible arithmetic. I would be more comfortable if we could choose a last shift together. A vague promise of support would not settle me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look at in the bank statements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d add up rent, food, medicine and the car before counting travel or gifts. Our children are adults now, so school costs are gone, but we still need money to visit them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children for support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d talk to family if we were truly short, and I believe families should help one another. I would first use the paid work I still have and make a clear budget with Peter.

say: I’d say **five years** helps only if the mine shares machine orders.
I’d ask for real **apprenticeships** for younger workers.
think: At **66**, stopping may be possible but depends on our retirement numbers.
Peter’s future **shop hours** are uncertain too.
do: Get a **retirement estimate** and list household costs with Peter.
Keep asking about **loader work** and continue paid shifts.
Compare **2032 bills** with any offered exit payment before signing.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to calculate the household gap over several years.
S3.quote: A vague promise of support would not settle me.
fieldNote: The later robot date might meet Chloe at **retirement age**, yet she refuses to treat age alone as proof of affordability.
Her request for **apprenticeships** concerns younger workers; for herself she plans to budget and keep paid shifts.

steps.text: Continue paid loader shifts while the mine offers them
Wait for written machine orders and exit terms before signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that ten years gives us a chance to finish proper shifts and teach apprentices safely. Thinking AI in 2036 could change the office, while loading robots arrive around 2039. I would be 71 at the robot date and hope to be out of the loader seat by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 when the thinking AI arrives. I do not know whether our retirement money will cover life at that age, but the long warning gives Peter and me time to check. I would rather leave after training a real apprentice than watch a machine take over an unexamined pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request updated retirement figures every year and keep the loader job while health and the roster allow. I’d show a new apprentice how to inspect bucket pins if the mine actually assigns one to me. In 2037 I’d check our household income against bills and retire if the figures work; otherwise I’d ask for shorter paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly calm about the robot reaching the loader after my likely working years. There is still uncertainty about money and health. I can live with that better when we have time to count things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool to teach the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the machine and a real inspection. A training screen could come later if the fitter has checked it, but I would not ask an apprentice to trust a fault code blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still write down the pin checks for the next operator. I cannot force the mine to hire anyone, and I would not count a mentoring role as income unless offered.

say: I’d say **ten years** allows safer handovers to apprentices.
I hope to leave the **loader seat** before robots arrive around 2039.
think: At **68** in 2036, retirement depends on household income, not my preferred date.
I want to pass on **inspection habits** before leaving.
do: Keep paid **loader shifts** while health and the roster allow.
Check **2037 income** against bills before retiring or seeking shorter shifts.
feel: **Calm** about a late robot date, with money and health still to check.
S4.quote: I would rather leave after training a real apprentice than watch a machine take over an unexamined pit.
fieldNote: Chloe expects the **2039 robot date** after her likely loader career, though retirement affordability remains unproved.
She wants to pass on **bucket pin checks** through a genuine apprentice assignment, without counting that work as guaranteed income.

steps.text: Keep paid loader shifts while health and the roster allow
Wait for 2037 income figures before deciding whether to retire

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because a loader robot could take my wages at 63. I want written dates, honest redundancy terms and a real vacancy list, not a promise to retrain everybody. Peter and I can make our own choices once the figures are on the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who keeps the next apprentice safe when the experienced operators leave. A loose bucket pin can look like nothing to somebody reading a screen. I want the person in that seat to know when to park the loader.

headlineQuote: A loose bucket pin can look like nothing to somebody reading a screen.
portrait: Chloe, **58**, operates a loader and relies on direct inspection rather than AI tools.
She and Peter have **four months** of bills saved and still need mine wages before retirement.
She resists unproved screens but would share **inspection skills** with a real apprentice.
Fast loading robots threaten her remaining **earning years**; a decade gives her time to check the retirement figures.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Chloe most because loading robots around 2031 could remove her wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Written **machine dates**, redundancy terms and a genuine vacancy list would let her plan with Peter.
